# Education in Greece
Education in Greece is structured into several stages: compulsory preschool, primary, and lower secondary education, followed by non-compulsory upper secondary education and tertiary (higher) education. Preschool is compulsory for children aged 4 to 6 and consists of one year of pre-kindergarten and one year of kindergarten, with English language instruction beginning at this stage. Primary school (Dimotiko) is compulsory for six years (ages 6–12), after which students automatically enroll in lower secondary education. Gymnasium (lower secondary) comprises three years (ages 12–15) and is also compulsory, with a strong emphasis on English and options for French or German. Completion of Gymnasium grants access to Lyceum (upper secondary), which is non-compulsory and lasts three years (ages 15–18), culminating in the Apolytirio Lykeiou (high school diploma) and eligibility for higher education entrance examinations (Pan-Hellenic Examinations).
Upper secondary education offers both general and vocational tracks, including various specialized lyceums and vocational schools (EPAL, EPAS, ESK, SAEK). Vocational pathways provide multiple diploma levels (HQF Level 4 and 5) and options for post-secondary apprenticeships, with flexible articulation to higher education. The education system is managed by the Ministry of Education and includes public, private, model, experimental, and special schools, as well as opportunities for lifelong learning and non-formal education. Higher education is predominantly provided by public universities and specialist academies, with recent legislation permitting private accredited institutions. Admission to tertiary education is based on national examinations and standardized criteria, and most public universities offer free tuition for undergraduate study, with limited fees for postgraduate programmes.
The National Qualification Framework (HQF) aligns both formal and vocational qualifications to European standards. Greece’s education sector includes supplementary programmes, such as lifelong learning centres and digital platforms for open online courses. Recent initiatives include the introduction of the International Baccalaureate in public schools and new policies for inclusive education and skills development. Despite reforms and expanding options, the sector faces challenges such as reported corruption, discipline concerns, and disparities in school conditions.
